claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.
upkeep_per_week.value: unknown; could be below or above the Child Benefit rate

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I'd be happy to help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. To assess your eligibility, I'll need to ask you some questions.

Let's start with the basics:

**Do you have any children, and if so, how many children are you inquiring about?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, I have one child I'm asking about - my son Alex. He's 18 and doesn't live with me anymore, but I'm wondering if I can still claim Child Benefit for him.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for providing that information about your son Alex. To help determine your eligibility for Child Benefit for Alex, I need to ask you some questions.

Since Alex is 18 and doesn't live with you anymore, let me ask:

**Is Alex currently in approved education or training?** (For example, is he in sixth form, college, studying for A-levels, or in another approved training program?)

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, he is. He's still in college doing his A-levels.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
That's helpful to know. Since Alex is in approved education (doing A-levels), that's a positive factor for eligibility even though he's 18.

Now, you mentioned Alex doesn't live with you anymore. Let me ask:

**Are you making any financial contributions towards Alex's upkeep?** (This could include things like money for food, clothes, pocket money, rent, or other living expenses)

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: I'm not really sure about the exact amount - it varies quite a bit. Some weeks I help out more than others, you know how it is.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I understand - contributions can vary. To help determine your eligibility, I need to understand a bit more about the contributions you're making.

**Can you give me a rough idea of what you typically contribute in a month?** (For example, do you give him money for food or rent regularly, buy him clothes, give him pocket money, or help with other expenses? Even an approximate total would be helpful)

Also, **how long has it been since Alex moved out and stopped living with you?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text:
Well, like I said, it really does vary week to week. Some weeks I might help with a bit of food money or clothes, other weeks I might not be able to. I honestly couldn't give you a typical amount - it just depends on what he needs and what I can afford at the time.

As for when he moved out, it's been a few months now.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for explaining that. I understand the situation better now.

Let me ask you this important question:

**When you do contribute, would you say the total amount you give Alex each week (or month) is at least as much as the Child Benefit payment?** 

For reference, Child Benefit is currently £25.60 per week (or about £102.40 per month) for an eldest or only child. 

So on average, considering the weeks when you do help and the weeks when you don't, **do your contributions add up to at least this amount?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: I really can't say for certain. Like I mentioned, it varies so much - some weeks I give more, some weeks nothing at all. I honestly don't know if it adds up to that amount on average or not. It's just not consistent enough for me to say either way.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I understand - thank you for being honest about your situation. Let me ask a couple more questions to complete my assessment:

1. **Is anyone else currently claiming Child Benefit for Alex?** (For example, is the person he's living with now claiming it?)

2. **Do you know approximately how many months ago Alex moved out?** (This will help me understand if it's been more or less than 8 weeks)

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text:
1. I don't think anyone else is claiming Child Benefit for him, no. The person he's living with hasn't mentioned anything about claiming it.

2. It's been a few months now - probably around 3 or 4 months, I'd say.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for providing all that information. Let me ask one final question to complete my assessment:

**Were you receiving Child Benefit for Alex before he moved out, or are you looking to make a new claim now?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: I'm looking to make a new claim now. I wasn't claiming it before he moved out.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Based on all the information you've provided, I'm unable to definitively determine whether you would be eligible for Child Benefit for Alex. Here's why:

**The positive factors:**
- Alex is 18 and in approved education (doing A-levels), which means he falls within the age criteria - Child Benefit can continue for children under 20 in approved education or training.

**The challenge:**
- Since Alex doesn't live with you and moved out 3-4 months ago (well beyond the initial 8-week period), your eligibility depends on whether you're contributing at least as much as the Child Benefit payment (£25.60 per week or about £102.40 per month) towards his upkeep.
- Because your contributions vary so much week to week and you're unable to confirm whether they add up to this amount on average, there isn't enough information to determine if you meet the "responsibility" test required for Child Benefit eligibility.

**My recommendation:**
You would need to contact HMRC Child Benefit Office directly to discuss your specific situation. They would assess whether your contributions are sufficient to qualify. It would be helpful if you could:
- Keep track of all contributions you make to Alex (money, clothes, food, etc.)
- Calculate whether these add up to at least the Child Benefit amount over time

Without being able to demonstrate that your contributions meet the required threshold, a claim may not be successful.

reasonings:
Alex is 18 years old and is in approved education (doing A-levels at college), which means he falls within the age criteria as Child Benefit can continue for children under 20 who stay in approved education or training.

However, there are significant issues regarding the responsibility test for Child Benefit eligibility:

1. Alex does not live with the claimant (moved out 3-4 months ago), so the 'living with the child' criterion is not met.

2. The claimant could potentially still qualify if they are contributing at least the same amount as Child Benefit (£25.60 per week or £102.40 per month) towards Alex's upkeep. However, the claimant has stated that their contributions vary significantly week to week, and they cannot confirm whether the contributions add up to at least the Child Benefit amount on average.

3. According to the rules, when a child goes to live with someone else, Child Benefit can usually continue for 8 weeks. After that, it can continue for longer if the claimant makes contributions to the child's upkeep that equal or exceed the Child Benefit amount. Since Alex moved out 3-4 months ago, this is well beyond the 8-week period.

4. This is a new claim (not a continuation of an existing claim), which adds complexity.

Without clear evidence that the claimant's contributions consistently meet or exceed the Child Benefit threshold amount, and given the claimant's uncertainty about the total value of their contributions, there is insufficient information to determine definitively whether they would meet the 'responsibility' test for Child Benefit eligibility. The claimant would need to be able to demonstrate to HMRC that their contributions equal or exceed the Child Benefit amount for their claim to be successful after the initial 8-week period has passed.

The claimant would need to provide clearer evidence of their contribution levels to HMRC for a definitive assessment.
